sources.title: Song Ho-jung, Gojoseon and the Lelang Commandery, A History of Korea (2019)
sources.note: Academy of Korean Studies publication, translated by Daniel Kane, chapter 1, especially printed pp. 24-31. PDF directly read. The 194 BCE accession is in the chapter timeline; p. 27 contains an apparent end/beginning-of-second-century translation error, not adopted. General geographical focus and historical ending are used; archaeological distributions are not treated as exact borders. Entire book URL has one combined budget.

sources.title: Song Ho Jung, The Formation of Gojoseon and Its Social Characteristics (2004)
sources.note: Original Review of Korean Studies 7.1, pp. 95-114, directly read. Pp. 97-100 discuss dolmens, regional alliance and limits of identifying one political structure from cultural similarity; pp. 103-105 discuss Wiman-period officials and trade. Interpretations are attributed, rather than presented as surviving government records.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History, Gojoseon’s growth and changes: the Weilüe account
sources.note: Direct original Classical Chinese excerpt, Korean translation and modern scholarly commentary. The Weilüe passage is preserved in commentary to Sanguozhi, book 30. Late-fourth-century royal title and minister Ye’s intervention are retrospective evidence; early-third-century Yan invasion follows. The recorded 2,000 li are not converted into a surveyed frontier.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History, Dangun’s story and the founding of Gojoseon
sources.note: Direct Samguk yusa book 1 excerpt, original Classical Chinese and Korean translation, plus commentary. Medieval transmission is explicit. The supernatural bear transformation is presented as a founding story, not medical, dietary or archaeological evidence. No historically verified founding year inferred.

sources.title: National Museum of Korea, Mandolin-shaped Bronze Dagger
sources.note: Direct museum exhibit description. Bipa-shaped outline, raised spine and separate manufacture of hilt and blade. This is a type description, not a precisely dated royal weapon or identified ruler’s property.

sources.title: Yi Kun-moo, The Bronze Culture of Korea (2007)
sources.note: Original National Museum of Korea journal article, DOI 10.23158/jkaa.2007.v1_01, read through extensive indexed original text because direct HTML/PDF fetch failed. Reproducible query: site.ijkaa.org "Misong-ri" "cave" returns sections II.1-2; query site.ijkaa.org/v.1/0/6/68 "mold" "Yeongheung" returns production and repair sections. Same-work PDF URLs share this budget. Regional Bronze Age material is not proof of exact Gojoseon sovereignty. Sincheon dagger handle is attributed provenance, not a documented excavation.

sources.title: National Museum of Korea, Gojoseon Pottery: Misongri type
sources.note: Direct museum description: first identified in the Misong-ri cave, form, stone-coffin burial contexts, distribution north of the Cheongcheon River and different contemporary pottery to its south.

sources.title: National Museum of Korea, Flowerpot-shaped Pottery
sources.note: Direct museum description: predominantly northwestern tomb finds, concentration in Daedong River region, coarse sand in clay and exterior soot interpreted as probable boiling use. No exact recipe, individual household or precise year supplied.

sources.title: Kim Dong-il, Livelihood Style of Bronze Age in Northeast Asia, volume 1 (2022)
sources.note: Korea Citation Index author abstract directly read in Korean and English. Gogogwangjang 31, pp. 33-78. Regional study of plant and animal remains in Liaoning/Jilin and comparison with northern Korea; direct northern Korean data access is expressly limited. No invented Gojoseon menu, exact household or claim that all regional sites belonged to the state.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History, Gojoseon’s Eight Prohibitions: Hanshu excerpt and commentary
sources.note: Direct Classical Chinese text from Hanshu book 28B, Geography, with Korean translation and modern commentary. The source describes Joseon people of Lelang in a later Han-dynasty account. Only three of eight rules are preserved here. The transmission and relation to local Han regulations remain debated. The writing sample is external/later Chinese, not an authenticated native Gojoseon text or reconstructed spoken language.

proposedOverrides.name: Gojoseon
proposedOverrides.summary: An early northern Korean and Liaodong polity, remembered through archaeology and later historical accounts.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One exact missing HB record, circa 400-323 BCE. No alias or new geometry. Public narrative extends into explicitly labelled later Wiman and post-conquest history, but imported dates remain map coverage.
limitations: Decoded multipolygon bounds 121.06-138.65 E and 36.56-47.11 N extend far beyond the historical focus in Liaodong/northwestern Korea. This is a material geometry problem, publicly warned in the opening, not certified as corrected.
The 323 BCE endpoint is not a fall. No fell event or successor link is manufactured inside the map window; actual conquest in 108 BCE is discussed in prose.
Dangun’s supernatural founding narrative survives in medieval works; it is not treated as an eyewitness account or an archaeologically demonstrated foundation in 2333 BCE.
Archaeological cultures, dolmen distributions and broad regional food studies are not identified automatically with the borders of one Gojoseon state.

Bronze production examples are placed in northern Bronze Age cultural context, not asserted to be royal commissions or assigned exact invented years. Sincheon handle provenance is attributed, not excavated.
Wiman administration and Hanshu law/family material are labelled later than the fourth-century map phase. The 45 BCE household register belongs to post-conquest Lelang.

Chinese literary evidence is external. No indigenous readable sentence, universal school system, specific healing recipe or sanitation installation was securely established in selected sources. No such features are invented.
